Thank you for the additional information. I remain clearly in favor of the paper and think this would be a clear contribution. I am glad to hear that the authors have good plans for the additional camera-ready page. 

Given the discussion of the statistical tests, I'm curious about specifically how Table 4 was done and I think it's probably worth making crystal clear in the paper. Unclear protocols cause drama later on (e.g., the Pascal VOC definition of AP), and if this isn't explained clearly, I can see lots of people doing this wrong and claiming wrong results (for the sake of clarity, I will add that I don't think that this is the case here).

To give concrete numbers, let's look at Table 4 and pick 12.2 ± 1.3 vs 13.2 ± 1.1? If I understand correctly from the paper, there are approximately N = 31.9 hours * 3600 seconds per hour * 60 frames per second = 6,890,400 data points. These N data points are spread across 20 users. I can see the Test in Table 4 being done in two ways,: 
- Option 1: a statistical test on *all* the errors (i.e., on N paired samples), which should produce some p value that's mind-numbingly small, like near floating point epsilon. 
- Option 2: a statistical test on 20 paired samples, one average error each user, which should produce some p value that's small but reasonable .

If it's option 2, that makes sense, but I suspect that lots of people will just implement option 1 and we'll end up with a host of papers that don't improve on results but then seem to have statistical evidence that they do.

If the paper is doing option 1, I'll explain why I think this is problematic in advance to avoid the dreaded delayed back and forth in NeurIPS reviewer/author discussions. The problem with the first option is that the test assumes samples are independent. Since the data points are captured sequentially at 60FPS, they're not independent at all. If a method fails at frame 100, it's far more likely that it will fail at frame 101 and at frame 99. As an extreme example: suppose one had a camera that captured at 600,000 fps (10,000 higher frame rate than the current setup) -- this doesn't increase the number of independent samples by a factor of 10,000. I don't have a great stats reference handy, but you can find a few discussions of this problem on statistics stack exchange here: 
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/78788/can-i-use-wilcoxon-signed-rank-test-to-test-pairs-of-data-in-a-time-series and https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/100439/can-i-use-wilcoxon-signed-rank-test-for-time-series-data .

rebuttal.value:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful comments, which will help strengthen the paper. We are pleased with the generally positive reception of our benchmarks, in particular with reviewers’ comments on the:
- scale and organization of our dataset, which addresses a “critical need in sEMG-based hand pose estimation”
- well designed test splits and metrics enabling rigorous testing of generalization across various axes
- detailed data analysis, results, and discussion
- thorough literature review and comparison with existing datasets

The most considerable areas for improvement mentioned by the reviewers were to:
- include more complex behaviors in our dataset such as hand-hand and hand-object interactions (reviewer cZ4K)
- implement more baselines from the literature (reviewer kNuk)
- explore more sophisticated architectures (reviewer kNuk)
- improve the low metric scores (reviewer cZ4K, reviewer NebK)

We respond to these additional reviewer comments in each rebuttal, providing new figures and tables in the additional individual pdfs. In summary, we:
- highlight that our dataset already includes hand-hand and hand-object interactions and share new analyses of these behaviors in reviewer cZ4K’s 1 pager pdf. We will modify the paper to highlight these.
- implemented an additional baseline [1], and report scores in reviewer kNuk’s 1 pager pdf. We will include this baseline in the paper and codebase.
- additionally explored transformer auto-regressive architectures, reporting scores in reviewer kNuk’s 1 pager pdf. We will also include this model in the paper and codebase.
- comment that our submission presents a challenging and unsolved task similar to the ‘FreiHand’ benchmark (hand-pose estimation from CV), which saw significant advancements over time despite providing a significantly smaller dataset than ours. We hope that our submission will spur innovation for both ML and HCI communities.

We look forward to addressing any further reviewer questions in the upcoming weeks.

[1] Sîmpetru, Raul C., et al. "Sensing the full dynamics of the human hand with a neural interface and deep learning." bioRxiv (2022): 2022-07.

We point the reviewer to the 1 page pdf for all **Updated Tables**.

> One worry that I have is hardware reproducibility … 

This is a fair and insightful point. We will discuss this more in a revised manuscript. As you mentioned, our dataset will be valuable as a testbench for new algorithms, and for guiding data collection requirements for sEMG via scaling laws (Figure 6). We feel confident that algorithms and modeling approaches developed using the benchmark will transfer favorably to commercially available hardware. Furthermore, the device we are using is also being shared with academic labs (e.g [1]), and we have plans to distribute it for research purposes more broadly. 

The restriction to bespoke hardware is a general limitation of machine learning for wearable devices, and also applies to the use of IMU sensors, stretch sensitive gloves, and other sEMG bands. While methods for cross-device transfer of models across sEMG devices are still in their infancy, they have been explored in EEG and these approaches are viable to be used with EMG [2-4]. 

[1] Despradel, Dailyn et al. “Realtime Detection and Decoding of Motor Unit Activity Using a Wearable Neuromotor Interface in a Person with Motor Complete Tetraplegia.” NCM2024.

[2] M. Nakanishi, et al, "Facilitating Calibration in High-Speed BCI Spellers via Leveraging Cross-Device Shared Latent Responses," in IEEE Trans.on Biomed.Eng., 2020

[3] Wei, Xiaoxi, et al. "2021 BEETL competition: Advancing transfer learning for subject independence and heterogenous EEG data sets." NeurIPS 2021..

[4] Yi, K., Wang, Y., Ren, K., & Li, D. (2024). Learning topology-agnostic eeg representations with geometry-aware modeling. NeurIPS

>Some of the experiment writeup is a bit difficult to read …

In the camera-ready version of the paper, given we have an additional page, we will move the analyses and figures from appendix sections D1-4 into the main text. Additionally, we will relocate parts of the "limitations" section to the appendix to make the paper easier to navigate and to enhance the clarity and interpretation of the figures.

> It may help to comment in Table 3 that the hours can add up across the row….

To clarify that the test sets are entirely separate and intended to measure different aspects of the problem, we:
Add the following sentence to the caption of Table 3: “Three separate test sets measure generalization to new users, new types of behavior (stages), and new users plus types of behavior (user and stage). Note that the overall hours is the sum of the hours across all splits.”
In section 3.4 we replace the sentence “In contrast, we provide three held-out evaluation settings covering all these axes” with the sentence “In contrast, we provide three separate test sets intended to measure these axes independently.”

> How did the Wilcoxon signed-rank test account for the strong correlations between the datapoints in Table 4? …

In Table 4 we ran six paired comparisons between NeuroPose and vemg2pose using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. There is no overlap between the three test sets (user, stage, stage and user). Therefore, there is no nested structure that needs to be accounted for. We believe Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are appropriate in this context, as they are non-parametric and make minimal assumptions about the data distribution.

To correct for multiple comparisons, we reran the tests using a Bonferroni correction. For the 6 tests in the Table, the p threshold was adjusted from .01 to .0016. All results remained significant.

We are happy to run additional corrections or alternative tests if the reviewer can kindly point us to the appropriate references.

> I sort of understand why the paper counts right and left hand captures as separate data [...], but there's something a little funny about this …

We counted left and right handed data separately because sEMG inputs to the model are per-hand, as are their joint angle targets. This will be clarified in the Dataset section. However, we agree that it would be more appropriate to pool data across both hands when comparing to camera-based datasets. To maximize transparency, Table 2 will be modified to include frame numbers when pooling across hands and not pooling across hands (see **Updated Table 2**).

We will also add the following sentence to Table 3 (which reports the number of hours in each data split) to highlight that we are counting left and right handed data separately: “The number of hours counts the right- left-handed data separately for each participant.”


> Can you help the reader understand what to look for in the accuracy?...

- Hand-pose estimation from sEMG poses challenges that are distinct from CV. We will add further discussion of this to the manuscript:
Because sEMG signals depend on a person’s physiology  (e.g. skin conductivity, muscle locations, muscles sizes), generalization is harder than CV. 
- sEMG is more closely related to angular accelerations than angular positions (unlike in CV). As such, sEMG predictions can be more prone to angular drift due to error accumulation (see the ring figure in Figure 14).
- Movement driven by intrinsic hand muscle activities, which originate and insert within the hand itself, could be harder to sense from wrist sEMG. Motions that result from such muscles include finger adduction/abduction. We have these motions in our corpus (Table 6; “neurips_supplementary_video.mp4” c.f. the vulcan gesture).
- Decodability can depend on muscle density. Figures 9 and 10 highlight how the location, number, and size of muscles affects regression performance. The thumb is easier to predict, and the pinky is harder. In addition distal joints are harder to predict than proximal (Figure 1).

> Some of the formatting is a bit unwieldy. Section 4 starts off with two tables.

We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We will reformat figures/tables to be more evenly distributed in the paper, closely aligned with the relevant text locations.

> Can you please compare your method with stress sensors or other flexible electronics for capturing gestures/pose estimations [1-4]

Thank you for noting these smart textile references. We will add 1, 2, and 4 to the related work section ‘Pose from other modalities’. We chose not to include 3 because of its focus on the lower body. We chose not to include these methods as a direct baseline as (1) most of these approaches focus on gesture recognition, rather than pose regression and (2) the added encumbrance of the glove on the hand make them appropriate for very different use cases compared to sEMG. 

> I am curious how you overcame the jitter of the collected signal when you processed the data. Any discussions on the pre/post processing you performed would be very appreciated.

We will expand upon the description of the pre and post processing used to capture ground truth joint angles in the revised version of the paper. Briefly, we used the approach described by [1], wherein markers on the hand are tracked via a commercial Optitrack system. They are then assigned to specific joints using a ConvNet, and an inverse kinematics solver produces the final joint angles. This approach performed very well relative to a baseline algorithm [2], particularly in the context of hand-hand and hand-object interactions (see Table 5 of their paper).

The original paper found it unnecessary to use regularization of the inverse kinematics procedure to ensure smoothness (see section 4.3). Nonetheless, we apply 15 Hz low pass filtering to the final joint angles to reduce any residual jitter. This cutoff is conservative relative to the cutoff of ~5Hz used elsewhere in the literature [3]. The mean absolute difference between the filtered and unfiltered signal was only 0.32 degrees on average across 500 recordings. We found that this cutoff frequency helped remove some minor jitter (**Additional Figure 1**).

[1] Han, Shangchen, et al. "Online optical marker-based hand tracking with deep labels." Acm transactions on graphics (tog) 37.4 (2018): 1-10.

[2] Alexanderson, Simon, Carol O’Sullivan, and Jonas Beskow. "Real-time labeling of non-rigid motion capture marker sets." Computers & graphics 69 (2017): 59-67.

[3] Ingram, James N., et al. "The statistics of natural hand movements." Experimental brain research 188 (2008): 223-236.

> The joint angle and variance still have large errors, it can be improved in the future.

Akin to many other benchmarks, this task is challenging and unsolved at its inception. Our hope is that the benchmark will spur innovations that improve performance on this and other tasks. Many prominent benchmarks were unsolved upon release, including ‘Imagenet’ [1] for image classification, ‘SQuAD2.0’ [2] for question and answering, ‘The Arcade Learning Environment’ [3] for reinforcement learning, and ‘FreiHand’ [4] for image-based hand-pose inference. Importantly, each of these benchmarks spurred remarkable advancements over time, to the point that some of them are considered “solved”. For ‘Imagenet’, top-1 accuracy improved from 68.3% to 92.4% [5]. For ‘SQuAD2.0’, Exact Match improved from 70.3% to 90.9% [6]. For ‘The Arcade Learning Environment’, on the Atari-57 benchmark, mean human normalized scores improved from 874% to 10.1k% [7].

‘FreiHand’ is particularly relevant as a CV hand pose estimation benchmark. The ‘FreiHand’ corpus contains only 32 subjects and 33k frames. In contrast, ours contains 193 subjects and 80M frames (40M for each hand of the user). In-fact, our corpus is competitive in scale to all the largest CV hand datasets (see Table 2 of the manuscript). In addition, ours is an order of magnitude larger than all other sEMG corpora (see Table 1 of the manuscript), the only one containing joint angle labels. Despite the small size of the FreiHand dataset, Procrustes Aligned Mean Per-Joint Position Error improved from 11mm to 5.7mm [8]. We believe releasing this benchmark to the community will enable improvements of similar magnitude to those observed for FreiHand.



[1] Deng, J., Dong, W., Socher, R., Li, L.-J., Li, K., & Fei-Fei, L. (2009). ImageNet: A large-scale hierarchical image database. In 2009 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 248-255). IEEE.

[2] Rajpurkar, P., Jia, R., & Liang, P. (2018). Know what you don't know: Unanswerable questions for SQuAD. arXiv preprint arXiv:1806.03822.

[3] Bellemare, M. G., Naddaf, Y., Veness, J., & Bowling, M. (2013). The arcade learning environment: An evaluation platform for general agents. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, 47, 253-279.

[4] Zimmermann, C., Ceylan, D., Yang, J., Russell, B., Argus, M., & Brox, T. (2019). Freihand: A dataset for markerless capture of hand pose and shape from single rgb images. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 813-822).

[5] https://paperswithcode.com/sota/image-classification-on-imagenet

[6] https://paperswithcode.com/sota/question-answering-on-squad20

[7] https://paperswithcode.com/sota/atari-games-on-atari-2600-venture

[8] https://paperswithcode.com/sota/3d-hand-pose-estimation-on-freihand

> Provide more details regarding motion capture setup, IK solver, and potential IK inaccuracies.

We will expand upon the data collection and annotation process in the camera ready. To determine joint angles from motion capture used the approach described by [1], which was shown to be accurate even under challenging occlusions (see their Table 5).

Briefly, 19 markers were attached to each hand, and their 3D coordinates were tracked via a commercial Optitrack system with 26 cameras around the participant on all sides. A ConvNet then assigned labels to each marker. The markers were registered to positions on a hand mesh to determine landmark positions. An inverse kinematics solver produced the final joint angles. We apply a conservative 15 Hz low pass filter to the final angles to ensure no residual jitter (**Additional Figure 1**). The mean absolute difference between filtered/unfiltered signal was only 0.32 degrees across 500 recordings.

[1] Han, Shangchen, et al. "Online optical marker-based hand tracking with deep labels." Acm transactions on graphics (tog) 37.4 (2018): 1-10.

> The selection of participants can bring bias.

We agree that recruiting a diverse group of participants is important for ensuring that EMG models can generalize to diverse unseen users. For these experiments we recruited participants with a broad span of age, height, weight, exercise levels, and other demographic factors. Demographic information is reported in Figure 5. In the revised manuscript we will additionally report demographics separately for the test set to make clear that models are evaluated on a diverse group of participants.

> Explore more advanced architectures like transformers.

We agree that additional architectures should be explored, and we hope our benchmark will provide a high quality proving ground for their development in the future. Nevertheless, to improve the manuscript we added a transformer baseline. We replaced the LSTM decoder with an auto-regressive torch.nn.TransformerEncoder(). We swept over num_layers (2, 4, 6), and nheads (2, 4, 8) and chose the best model for both tracking and regression tasks. We needed to cut the feature dimensionality of the transformer in half compared to the LSTM to fit in memory.

The transformer performs similarly to or slightly worse than the LSTM (**Additional Table 1**). We suspect the lack of performance gains is due to the scale of our dataset. The literature suggests that transformers only start to outperform in larger data-regimes [1,2,3]. We will include these new results in the appendix.

[1] Zeyer, Albert, et al. "A comparison of transformer and lstm encoder decoder models for asr." 2019 IEEE Auto. Speech Recog. and Under. (ASRU). IEEE, 2019.

[2] Sheikh, Imran Ahamad, Emmanuel Vincent, and Irina Illina. "Transformer versus LSTM language models trained on uncertain ASR hypotheses in limited data scenarios." LREC 2022. 2022.

[3] Ezen-Can, Aysu. "A Comparison of LSTM and BERT for Small Corpus." arXiv:2009.05451 (2020).

> A broader comparison to previous sEMG-based hand pose estimation methods.

In the manuscript we cite the most prominent two papers on sEMG to Pose - NeuroPose and SensingDynamics [1] - and implemented NeuroPose as a baseline. For the rebuttal, we have additionally implemented ‘SensingDynamics’. 

SensingDynamics was designed for a high-density sEMG device with 320 electrodes spread over 5 separate patches on the forearm and wrist. The architecture uses 3d convolutions over channels, patches, and time. Our device does not have separate patches, so we used 2d convolutions instead. Our device also has different channel densities and temporal sampling, so we modified the kernel, stride, and dilations to match respective receptive fields. We swept over learning rate and kept all other hyperparameters consistent with vemg2pose. ‘SensingDynamics’ was designed for regression, so we only evaluate it on the regression task.

‘SensingDynamics’ performance trails both vemg2pose and NeuroPose (**Additional Table 2**). This is perhaps not surprising: 1) All methods were evaluated on our 16 electrode device, but SensingDynamics was optimized for a high-density device with 320 electrodes; 2) SensingDynamics has a receptive field of only 94ms, which is smaller than NeuroPose’s 160ms and vemg2pose’s 5590ms. We have observed that significantly longer receptive fields than those used in SensingDynamics are necessary for good performance. We will include this additional baseline in the paper and codebase.   

[1] Sîmpetru, Raul C., et al. "Sensing the full dynamics of the human hand with a neural interface and deep learning." bioRxiv (2022).

> Discussion on how well these methods might generalize to real-world scenarios.

We thank the reviewer for promoting this relevant discussion that we will include in the updated manuscript.The challenging generalization scenarios included in the paper are intended to monitor the distributional shifts between training and evaluation that are likely to occur in real-world scenarios. Our benchmark includes broad variability in behavior, user physiologies and device placements that are the dominant source of variability in sEMG signals.

Nevertheless, one could encounter a range of additional signal aggressors “in the wild”, such as electrode-skin contact artifacts, impedance changes from sweat; electrical interference from external devices or non-stationary p(pose|emg) due to muscle fatigue. While these aggressors play a more minor role in sEMG variability, they may be important to include in future datasets. 


> The dataset is not publicly available.

The dataset and codebase are available to all reviewers and will be made available to the community upon camera-ready submission, as described in Appendix A Datasheet ‘Distribution and Maintenance’ section as well as in the supplementary materials’ ‘emg2pose_instructions.pdf’.

> I do not think the authors completely show the limitations of the vision-based system: for example, authors may need to tackle more complex scenarios having hand-hand and hand-object interactions where the occlusion becomes the real problem in vision-based systems… authors may need to conduct experiments regarding more challenging scenarios involving the hand-hand or hand-object interactions to validate the initial assumptions mentioned

We agree that the paper will benefit from increased attention drawn to behaviors that are known to be challenging for vision-based systems. Fortunately, our dataset includes behaviors specifically designed for this purpose, including (1) stages with interactions between both hands, (2) stages with hand-object interactions, and (3) stages in which the hand is not visible for headset based computer-vision systems. The revised version of the paper will include the following new analyses that draw attention to these conditions.

We find that stages with hand-hand interactions (tapping fingers together, clapping hands, sliding fingers along the opposite palm) or hand-object interactions (moving blocks, moving chess pieces, drinking from a cup, squeezing a toy) have similar model performance compared to stages without such interactions (**Additional Figure 1**). Although the comparison is imperfect (as the behavioral distribution differs between the interaction and non-interaction stages) this supports the feasibility of sEMG based hand tracking in the context of hand-hand and hand-object interactions. More importantly, the presence of these conditions in our benchmark will allow the community to make progress on behaviors known to be particularly challenging in other hand tracking contexts.

sEMG is particularly well suited to complement vision-based system during hand occlusion. As expected, we find that visual occlusion does not impact sEMG based pose reconstruction (**Additional Figure 2**). Stages in which the hand is occluded from a CV based headset tracking system have similar accuracy compared to stages without occlusion in which the same behaviors are performed.

The circumstances that are challenging for vision-based systems are distinct from those that are most challenging for sEMG. For example, the location, number, and size of muscles controlling different joints affects our ability to accurately predict the position of those joints. The thumb is therefore easier to predict, and the pinky is harder (**Figure 9**). Similarly, distal joints are more challenging than proximal joints (**Figure 10**).

Importantly, hand pose estimation from sEMG remains a challenging and unsolved task. The spirit of this benchmark is to provide the community the tools to monitor and make progress on this task, particularly for behaviors that are known to be challenging for other hand tracking systems.

summary_and_contributions.value: The authors introduce emg2pose, the first large-scale, publicly available dataset of high-quality hand pose labels and wrist sEMG recordings. With 193 users, 370 hours of data, 29 diverse kinematic stages, and more than 80M frames, this dataset is comparable in scale to leading computer vision hand pose datasets.

review.value:
Pros:

1. The paper presents two benchmark tasks - pose regression and pose tracking - with evaluation on held-out users, stages, and user-stage combinations. This allows for rigorous testing of generalization capabilities across different axes.

2. The paper includes detailed analyses of model performance across different fingers, joints, and stages. It also examines the impact of dataset scale on generalization and compares velocity-based vs. positional predictions.

3. The introduction of the emg2pose dataset, which is large-scale, diverse, and publicly available, addresses a critical need in the sEMG-based hand pose estimation research community.

Cons:

1. While the authors mention that existing datasets are small and not open-sourced, a more broader comparison of results with previous sEMG-based hand pose estimation methods would strengthen the paper.

2. Although the paper provides two baselines, it does not explore more advanced architectures like transformers or diffusion models that have shown promise in related fields.

3. The postprocessing of IK can be inaccurate, more discussions on how to solve this are needed.

4. The data collection and annotation process could be described in more detail, particularly regarding the motion capture setup and the IK solver used for joint angle reconstruction.

strengths.value: The main strengths lie in the scale of the dataset, and the potential impact on human-computer interaction research.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. The dataset is not publicly available.

2. The paper focuses on controlled laboratory settings. Discussion on how well these methods might generalize to real-world scenarios with varying conditions would enhance the work.

ethics.value: The selection of participants can bring bias.

summary_and_contributions.value: Authors proposed the hand pose estimation benchmark that uses the sEMG (surface electromyography)-based sensor. The dataset is capturing 2kHz, 16 channel sEMG and pose labels from 15 a 26-camera motion capture rig for 193 users, 370 hours, and 29 stages with 16 diverse gestures. Experiments are conducted for real-world generalization scenarios and demonstrate the effectiveness of the method.

review.value:
(+) Authors proposed the dataset which uses relatively under-explored sensors. 
(-) Seeing the video demo, the obtained results are seemingly not very good yet. More dataset might have to be collected.
(-) Also, there could be more challenging scenarios involving more interaction cases.

strengths.value: Compared to vision-based approaches, the sEMG-based sensor has advantages for occluded signals and lighting. Authors proposed a dataset which is large in scale and publicly available. This could be a significant contribution to the community.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
Seeing the video demo, the predicted results involve much error.

The paper is worth to be publicized in the sense that the paper is tackling the new aspect; however I do not think the authors completely show the limitations of the vision-based system: for example, authors may need to tackle more complex scenarios having hand-hand and hand-object interactions where the occlusion becomes the real problem in vision-based systems. The future work may need to tackle such aspect.

limitations.value: The paper limitation is sufficiently discussed.

correctness.value: In general the paper conducted experiments in a correcy way; however as mentioned previously, authors may need to conduct experiments regarding more challenging scenarios involving the hand-hand or hand-object interactions to validate the initial assumptions mentioned.

clarity.value: The paper is well presented. Figures and tables are useful to understand the overall paper.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The prior works are sufficiently discussed.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces a dataset for estimation from electromyography that hopefully can test generalization. The data is collected with a new wristband that measures electrical potentials (sEMG) generated during motion. The data is collected by simultaneously capturing hands in a mocap setup and capturing sEMG data. 193 participants are captured over 370 hours (or maybe 185? if this the left+right hands are grouped). The paper presents two methods and does an analysis of how well they work.

review.value: Overall this paper is a good contribution to the literature. On the plus side, the dataset is large, has been done right, and will spur innovation. On the other hand, some of the writing is not clear.

strengths.value:
+ This dataset will be a good contribution to the community. Even if the hardware isn't broadly available, such a dataset may lead to innovations in how to do hand tracking and provide a proof of concept and proving ground for ideas. The data is large and has been thoughtfully gathered. The splits and metrics reflect good design decisions and so research on this data will be valuable. 

+ The paper does an overall good job of explaining the problems. Up until the experiments, the paper is clear and does a good job of introducing the particular challenges for this data.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- Some of the experiment writeup is a bit difficult to read (especially Lines 270 - 292). Roughly as much time is spent on discussing limitations as discussing experiments, which makes the paper harder to read
(a) There are many results that are deferred to the supplement in a way that's not great. It's ok if there's a conclusion, with backing data in the supplement. I think this is made worse by the combined main + appendix paper, where a figure may seem like it's close, but it's actually far away. In general, a lot of the paper requires flipping back and forth. 
(b) The paper would benefit from a bit more analysis. For example, there are two results figures (Fig 1 and 4). Can you help the reader understand what to look for in the accuracy? I've spent a lot of time with hands, so I can spot a few of the issues, but for sEMG-based outputs, I presume there are different problems

- I don't know the roadmap for the product that's being used for this effort, but one worry that I have is hardware reproducibility since the device isn't commercially available. Put another way, this can easily end up being a dataset that is designed for hardware that nobody has access to. This is usually isn't a concern for images/videos/text where the content itself carries obvious meaning. Even if the capture setups are confidential, the images/videos/text. are usually helpful because models trained on one sort of image generalize to others. **However**, I dos till think the paper still has value even without broad hardware availability -- hopefully it can be a proving ground for learning recipes, as opposed to a way to generate models.

limitations.value: Yes. The limitations are addressed quite clearly. I do think they could be shortened in favor of longer experiments.

correctness.value: - How did the Wilcoxon signed-rank test account for the strong correlations between the datapoints in Table 4? If no correction is done for the dependence between the datapoints, the test is wrong. I don't finding a significant difference between the two methods is critical for the paper, but I suspect that no correction has been done (since one would have to mention the effective number of samples) and therefore the test is not appropriate.

clarity.value:
- The splits are important and I trust that the authors have done them correctly. However, it takes a little bit of time to understand. It may help to comment in Table 3 that the hours can add up across the row. Or, since these sets are really entirely separate test sets, it may be helpful to frame them as three test sets testing three different things.

- Some of the writing of the experiments would benefit from another pass. For instance, throughout 272 - 303, the writing just drops Figure comments in sentences without trying integrating things in.

ethics.value: No. The data has been collected in a way that makes me not particularly concerned.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
Small stuff that doesn't impact my review:

- I sort of understand why the paper counts right and left hand captures as separate data (since that's what it seems like to the task proposed in the dataset), but there's something a little funny about this when comparing with other datasets. My understanding is that this is because the data used in the method is per-hand. But then when one compares with a camera-based dataset, it's a little funny.

- Some of the formatting is a bit unwieldy. Section 4 starts off with two tables.

title.value: emg2pose: A Large and Diverse Benchmark for Surface Electromyographic Hand Pose Estimation

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper is interesting, which contains 2kHz, 16 channel sEMG and pose labels from a 26-camera motion capture rig for 193 users, 370 hours, and 29 stages with diverse gestures. The paper provides competitive baselines and challenging tasks evaluating real-world generalization scenarios: held-out users, sensor placements, and stages. This provides a platform for exploring complex generalization problems, holding the potential to significantly enhance the development of sEMG-based human-computer interactions.

review.value: This is a high-quality D&B paper I have reviewed so far, with a good literature review and comparison with public datasets. Based on the rich data, analysis, results and discussion. I would suggest to accept this paper.

strengths.value: This paper provides two baselines: an open-source re-implementation of the NeuroPose network architecture and vemg2pose model

opportunities_for_improvement.value: The joint angle and variance still have large errors, it can be improved in the future.

limitations.value:
Can you please compare your method with stress sensors or other flexible electronics for capturing gestures/pose estimations [1-4]? Also I am curious how you overcame the jetter of the collected signal when you processed the data. Any discussions on the pre/post processing you performed would be very appreciated. This is still not clear in the main text.

[1] Tashakori, Arvin, et al. "Capturing complex hand movements and object interactions using machine learning-powered stretchable smart textile gloves." Nature Machine Intelligence (2024): 1-13.

title.value: emg2pose: A Large and Diverse Benchmark for Surface Electromyographic Hand Pose Estimation

TLDR.value: We present the first large scale surface electromyography hand pose dataset for generalized hand pose inference solely from wrist-based wearables.

abstract.value: Hands are the primary means through which humans interact with the world. Reliable and always-available hand pose inference could yield new and intuitive control schemes for human-computer interactions, particularly in virtual and augmented reality. Computer vision is effective but requires one or multiple cameras and can struggle with occlusions, limited field of view, and poor lighting. Wearable wrist-based surface electromyography (sEMG) presents a promising alternative as an always-available modality sensing muscle activities that drive hand motion. However, sEMG signals are strongly dependent on user anatomy and sensor placement; existing sEMG models have thus required hundreds of users and device placements to effectively generalize for tasks other than pose inference. To facilitate progress on sEMG pose inference, we introduce the emg2pose benchmark, which is to our knowledge the first publicly available dataset of high-quality hand pose labels and wrist sEMG recordings. emg2pose contains 2kHz, 16 channel sEMG and pose labels from a 26-camera motion capture rig for 193 users, 370 hours, and 29 stages with diverse gestures - a scale comparable to vision-based hand pose datasets. We provide competitive baselines and challenging tasks evaluating real-world generalization scenarios: held-out users, sensor placements, and stages. This benchmark provides the machine learning community a platform for exploring complex generalization problems, holding potential to significantly enhance the development of sEMG-based human-computer interactions.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
